turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it’s Monday, the twenty-first of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let’s go.
Today: three governments confirmed the same agreement on Friday. Not one of them has published it.
[curious] Published what, exactly? There’s no text?
There is no text. Anywhere.
Also: Singapore has a haze law it has never once used. Twelve years, no investigation.
And in Vietnam, shopkeepers are taking the QR codes off their counters. Deliberately.
[amused] Going backwards. On purpose. Where do we start?
The Arctic.
Greenland. What do we actually know?

Washington, Copenhagen and Nuuk all confirmed a deal on Friday. The Danish prime minister’s office put out a release headed — sit with this — “Expected agreement.” Four days before a signing. It ends: there are no further comments at this time.
[deadpan] Stirring.
Donald Trump was less procedural. He wrote that the United States now has permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland — and that no adversary can ever hold a base there.
So Copenhagen says sovereignty recognised, Washington says permanent control. Same document.
The document nobody has read.
[skeptical] Then where are the specifics coming from?

One place. United States officials briefing one American broadcaster. Permanent basing and overflight with no expiry. New installations on consultation rather than consent. China and Russia barred from bases, and from investing in telecoms, cables, ports and critical minerals. We print all of it as single-sourced, because that’s what it is.
And the sceptic?

Peter Viggo Jakobsen, of the Royal Danish Defence College, told Danish public radio the Americans have been handed rights they already held under the nineteen fifty-one defence treaty. His line: congratulations Trump — you now have what you’ve had since the nineteen fifties, when the base agreement was signed.
[gasps] So it’s a rerun.

He calls the annexation campaign more theatre than genuine military concern. And the footprint supports him. At the Cold War’s height, seventeen installations and more than ten thousand troops. Now one base — about a hundred personnel.
[pause] And the Greenlanders?
Fifty-six thousand people. In January of last year, eighty-five per cent opposed becoming American. Nobody asked them this time either.
[wry] Permanent control of what, though.
That’s the question only the unpublished text answers. And one more from that desk: Germany held two state elections, and a governing party polled four point nine per cent and left with nothing.
[curious] Nothing?

A tenth of a point below the threshold, so zero seats. Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats — their worst state result anywhere since the war, an exit from a parliament rather than a defeat inside one. Though the decimals are preliminary; the exit polls corroborate the order, not the last digit.
Home. The haze.
Singapore has a law for this. In twelve years it has opened no investigation.
Not one?

Not one. The Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, twenty-fourteen: an offence to cause or contribute to haze pollution here, wherever the fire is lit. In February the environment minister Grace Fu told Parliament no investigation had ever been initiated — because the haze has not reached such levels which would warrant investigation. The peak she cited was sixty-nine.
And six days ago?
All five regions unhealthy at once for the first time since twenty-nineteen. Central read a hundred and fifty-four.
[pause] Sixty-nine, to a hundred and fifty-four.
That answer is seven months old and has not been revisited. At a hundred and fifty-four, does it now warrant investigation? Nobody has been asked. And nobody has said.
Where is it this morning?

We read the agency’s feed at three — the moderate band, better than the week has been. And it was forecast. The Singapore Institute of International Affairs rated the risk Red in June, its highest band, and named August to September as the window.
But the sceptic argues against reaching for the statute.

The same forecast does. Their associate director points at demand rather than carelessness — the fuel crisis is driving demand for biofuels, with Southeast Asian countries increasing the percentage of vegetable oil in diesel.
So a blending mandate is a price signal on palm oil—
—and therefore on land. Which makes the burning a regional policy output rather than a local crime.
[amused] And from smoke to money.

Where diversification stopped working in all four directions at once. Stocks and bonds have moved together for a month — daily-return correlation plus nought point five seven over twenty-one sessions. Every leg lost money last week, and gold ended twenty-one point eight per cent below its January high.
That’s not a bad week for a sixty-forty.

It’s the signature of an inflation-shock regime. And the cause is one variable: three central banks raised rates inside eight days, all reacting to energy. American headline inflation ran at three point four per cent in August, energy up sixteen point three on the year.
So the energy number sets the reaction function—
—which sets real yields, and real yields set the dollar. The ten-year touched five point nought four per cent intraweek, its highest since two thousand and seven.
[wry] And the name for it?

Energy-shock re-tightening. While oil is the marginal driver of the headline print, bonds will not hedge equities — they’ll amplify them, repriced by the same discount rate rather than by growth. Gold trades as a real-rates asset, not an inflation hedge. So the thing to watch is not the Fed. It’s Brent. Explanation, not advice.
And there’s a correction on page two.

Ours. Yesterday we printed the American ten-year at four point nine nine seven per cent under a note saying the yields were on the par curve. They weren’t — that was the market close. The Treasury’s own par yield that day was four point nine three.
[warmly] Say it and move on. Technology, then — Firefox.

Firefox’s browsing assistant is now powered by Mistral models. Mozilla published that on the sixteenth. Four paragraphs — and it doesn’t name the models, or say where the inference runs. No benchmark, no version number, no word on Singapore.
But zero data retention.

Which is a promise about what is kept — not about where the text goes first. And for a European-sovereignty pitch arriving in the last independent browser, the location of the compute isn’t a detail. It’s the claim.
[thoughtful] So the practical answer is the one they don’t address.

Point the application at an endpoint you control. And the sceptic on that page is the sharpest thing in the window — Jay Kruer’s frame for a frontier model: a cracked intern. Quick and effective in the hands of an adult, but not given run of the place.
[laughs] That’s the most accurate thing I’ve heard all month.

And the analogy is from silicon. A processor project typically employs three times as many specification and validation engineers as design engineers. Rigorous specification is the expensive part of building anything correct — and a model that writes the design does not remove it.
The Kit. The watch shipped.

Apple Watch Ultra four — eleven hundred and ninety-nine Singapore dollars, read off Apple’s own store. What changed is the sensing: it samples heart rate every five seconds all day, and the reviewer who measures these things calls the optical sensor the best Apple has ever made.
So what’s the catch?
[deadpan] It samples every five seconds. It shows you one reading in five.
[scoffs] Go on.

Apple records only points meeting its internal quality confidence levels — which produces gaps of twenty seconds and more during hard efforts. Precisely when the reading matters, and precisely the interval a chest-strap comparison would expose. For a buyer replacing an Ultra two, the sensor is the reason. There is no other.
The Atelier. Buy it once — what’s on the bench?
The lamp on your desk. And the sentence to take away: a lamp with an unreplaceable LED has a service life, not a lifetime.
[curious] So the socket is the spec.

And it’s never on the front of the box. Nor is the number that matters on colour — the rendering index is the mean of only the first eight test colours, all pastels. Deep red is calculated and left out, and a blue-pump white LED has its trough exactly where deep red lives.
So a lamp can advertise a high score and be telling the truth.

Ask for the deep-red figure in writing. And fifty thousand hours isn’t a measurement either — it’s a projection to seventy per cent of output, a threshold chosen because people fail to notice the loss until well past it. What kills the lamp is the driver.
There’s a shop test in the chatter. I loved this.

From a thread on eye strain. One poster corrects the room in a line: no, the diodes don’t — the drivers do. Another gives the test. A fast phone-camera shutter, pointed at the lit page. If there are black lines across the screen, there’s a flicker problem.
[excited] You can do that in the shop. Today. And the white-label truth?

Anglepoise is a British design made in China for every model but the Giant, hand-built in Portsmouth. And the Paul Smith version at four hundred and thirty US dollars is the three-hundred-and-twenty-dollar lamp in different paint.
[laughs] There’s the logo tax, in one line. Right — take my hand. We’re going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] Knife making. Go.
Everything they argue about is one trade-off: how hard, against how tough. Steel names, quench recipes, twenty-year forum feuds — all of it is a position on one axis.
And making one is, what, four steps?

Four problems stacked. Shape — cut the outline from a flat bar, or hammer it hot. Geometry — grind the flats into a bevel, symmetrical, with a crisp transition where it stops; that’s the part that takes years. Heat treatment — heat past the critical temperature, quench fast enough to trap the steel hard and brittle, then temper it back to buy toughness. And the handle.
Which one makes or ruins it?
Step three. And it leaves no mark you can see.
[pause] Oh. That’s the whole hobby, isn’t it.
It’s why the economy runs on trust. Hold that.
How do people get in?

The doors are worn smooth. The first is a railroad spike — free steel that looks like a knife, and a Georgia supplier runs a spike-forging class at two hundred US dollars. Spike steel is too low in carbon to harden properly.
[laughs] So the hobby recruits you by disappointing you.

Falling in love with one and then finding it won’t hold an edge is the on-ramp to metallurgy. The second door is a weekend class, and the third is television — one channel with a million subscribers, at once the hobby’s biggest recruiter and its most reliable irritant.
There’s a ratio in here I keep thinking about.

Alec Steele, who hits hot steel on camera: one point six seven million subscribers. Knife Steel Nerds, the channel of the metallurgist who designed the alloy everyone argues about: forty-four thousand nine hundred.
[wry] And that’s not a complaint.

Spectacle recruits. The metallurgy keeps the people spectacle brought in. And the institutions are older than the internet — the American Bladesmith Society, founded nineteen seventy-six. There are a hundred and fourteen living Master Bladesmiths.
A hundred and fourteen. In the world.
In the world.
Now — the steel supply story. This is the one that got me.

Two mills closed six months apart, and you can see it on a product page today. Crucible Industries ceased operations last year, ending American powder production of its line. A German mill shut on the thirty-first of October, taking four simple carbon steels with it. Two of them are out of stock in every size at the biggest beginner supplier in America — we read the page yesterday.
[gasps] A furnace closing last October, arriving on a shopping cart this September.

Their own warning: once supplies run out, some alloys may not be returning for a long time. If at all. So if you want one of those blades — buy it when you see it. And then there’s a twist. MagnaCut is now pressed in Sweden, and when the metallurgist who designed it tested the new supply against the original in January, the European version showed significantly higher toughness.
[excited] So the American mill died, and the replacement is better.
And almost nobody knows it.
The gear. What’s the one big purchase?

The grinder. Two-by-seventy-two, not one-by-thirty — it’s the industrial belt size, so every abrasive exists in it, and a longer loop runs cooler. A Torus is eight hundred and forty-five US dollars assembled, with the motor and drive fourteen ninety-five on top. But the consumable isn’t steel. Ceramic belts run five to twenty dollars each, and a knife eats six to ten.
[exhales] So what does that come to?
One knife a month is five to eight hundred dollars a year. A forty-dollar bar of steel makes four knives — and the belts to grind them cost more than the bar.
[laughs] Of course they do.
And the argument of this September is about fakes. The Damascus fight is no longer whether pattern-welding performs. It’s whether the Damascus is real.
How do you tell?

A maker posting as Black Mamba Knives gives the tells: an acid-etched pattern sits on the surface, so a real one must continue over the spine and the choil. And the two faces of a forged billet are never identical — if the pattern is mirror perfect, it came from one file, not from the anvil.
Now tell me about the Journeyman test.

Every part of it is a proxy for something invisible. A Master Smith administers it, on a blade the candidate forged alone — no other person physically assisting. Once it begins, no work, not even light stropping, may be done to the blade.
What does he have to do?

Cut a free-hanging one-inch sisal rope through in one stroke — that’s edge geometry. Chop a two-by-four through twice, after which any nicks, chips, flat spots or rolled edges fail it. Then shave hair. With the part he chopped with.
[gasps] The same section of edge?

The same section. And then the vice. He bends his own blade ninety degrees. It may crack at the edge, but not more than a third of the way through. If anything breaks off, he fails — and waits six months.
[whispers] Six months.
The bend demonstrates a soft spine and a hard edge in one blade. And there’s a reversal I love: Damascus is forbidden for the Journeyman test, and mandatory for the Master.
Prove the knife works before you make it beautiful.

That’s the ladder in one line. And then the trust problem, which is real. In March, Bark River Knives closed after model runs were made with Chinese steel stamped as American. The admission is the founder’s own.
[sighs] So the buyer simply cannot check.

Every claim in this hobby — every steel name, every hardness number — is unverifiable without a spectrometer and a hardness tester. Though the metallurgist does settle the marketing argument, in both directions: premium steels are genuinely different, and a budget steel matched a premium one when the edge angles differed.
Geometry beats alloy.
Thirty-four dollars of simple carbon ground thin out-cuts a hundred and fifty-five dollars of MagnaCut ground thick.
So — ninety days, from Singapore. Realistically.

Singapore rules out most of the forge. No garage, no open flame, no high-voltage circuit. Book a class at Tombalek in Sungei Kadut, the only forge here open to the public. Then stock removal — carbon steel, Micarta, pins, epoxy, files and sandpaper, about three hundred and thirty Singapore dollars, and no fire at any point.
And only then—
Only if you’re still in at day ninety does a grinder make sense. And the expensive mistake there is electrical: get it in writing that the drive is rated for our mains frequency.
[warmly] That’s a genuinely useful last line.
Culture, and the body. Start with the Emmys — a freshman comedy won fourteen.
[curious] Fourteen?

An all-time record for a comedy series — and its critics’ aggregate is seventy-eight, the lowest of the night’s winners. Matthew Rhys also became the first person ever to take two lead acting Emmys in the same year.
And the critics?

The spread is the story. The Guardian’s Lucy Mangan filed a hundred — rich and wonderful, grownup, funny, scary, true. Slate’s Sam Adams filed forty, on a specific charge: the supporting cast is never developed, so the stakes never land.
A hundred, and a forty, averaging to seventy-eight.

And the mean is the one number that describes none of them. Meanwhile the major labels opened a second front twice in one week — Universal against a distributor, then Universal and Sony suing Suno again, over sixty thousand two hundred and two recordings.
The line from that filing?
Training a new model on the outputs of an infringing model does not eliminate the infringement. It launders it.
[pause] That’ll be quoted for years. Family desk — the phone at twelve.

A study of three thousand four hundred and eighty-six children who had no phone at twelve. Half of them got one. Outcomes measured at thirteen — adjusted for each child’s own score on the same measure before the phone arrived.
So they’re matched against themselves.

A year earlier. Internalizing symptoms, attention and total problem scores were worse in the acquiring group. Sleep fell, bedtime use rose. What didn’t move: academic performance, exercise, bullying and cyberbullying.
And the number you won’t print.

Any number describing how big this is. The paper isn’t typeset and the abstract publishes probability values only — no effect sizes, no minutes of sleep. In a cohort this large, that’s fully compatible with a real effect that is small.
[thoughtful] And the mediation result cuts against the headline.

It does. The indirect effects run through screen time, through holding a social-media account, and through bedtime use. Not through owning a handset. And on the other page, England put restrictive phone policies into twenty schools and costed the result. The wellbeing gain straddled zero. What they saved was ninety-four pounds a pupil a year in staff time.
[deadpan] The ban works. On the staffing budget.

Candice Odgers has been making the harder argument for years: caregiver mental health is the strongest predictor of teen mental health, by far. Note where she and the paper agree. Not on the handset. On the account, and the hour.
[exhales] That’s the uncomfortable one.
And in the diary: eighteen days to the street circuit. Satay by the Bay closes on the first of October — go this week or not at all.
[pause] The Undercurrent. Vietnam.
Không nhận chuyển khoản. We don’t accept bank transfers. Handwritten, taped to a till — in the country that grew QR payment value eighty-five per cent in a year.
[thoughtful] That’s a remarkable sentence.

The signs went up in June last year, and then the QR codes came off the counters. A shopkeeper with no lobbyist, no association and no column has exactly one lever — the decision about how money enters the shop.
And what were they refusing?
Not a tax. A record.
Walk me through it.

A decree obliged household businesses above a revenue threshold to issue electronic invoices from cash registers wired directly to the tax authority. Seven months later, Vietnam abolished the lump-sum tax that had stood for more than thirty years — for five million household businesses that supply thirty-nine per cent of the country’s jobs.
And what does the new system cost them?

The finance ministry’s own arithmetic. The average lump-sum payment was about seven hundred thousand dong a month. The average under declaration is about four point six million. Their words: nearly seven times higher.
[gasps] Seven times. Same shop?

Same shop, same street, same bowl of phở. The ministry published that as proof the old system let the larger operators pay least. Read from the counter, it’s a notice of a sevenfold increase arriving with a bookkeeping requirement attached.
And the response?

Immediate and physical — eighty per cent of shops closed in one province’s largest market. Then the measurable part. Between September and the end of January, cash in circulation as a share of total means of payment rose from nine point four eight per cent to eleven point five two. Roughly three hundred and sixty trillion dong walked out of the banking system in four months.
[whispers] Out of the banking system.

And a second series says it from the other side. Cashless payments rose thirty-eight per cent by volume and only fourteen by value. Many more transactions, far less money moving through them — precisely the shape you’d expect if small purchases stayed digital and larger ones went back to notes.
Did the state notice?
It saw it and pressed harder — a dispatch in March instructing provinces to promote cashless payment in order to improve tax management.
[skeptical] That’s the quiet part. In an official document.

Then, nine days after ordering every household business to declare its bank accounts, the state retreated: a decree raised the taxable threshold, backdated, taking two and a half million businesses out of the net at a self-costed loss of sixteen point six five trillion dong.
[exhales] They published the price of their own retreat.

It’s rare to see a government do that. And the second order is the one nobody in Hanoi has published. The bill isn’t landing on the tax office. It’s landing on the banks — what left was the cheapest deposits they hold, and they replace it with dearer funding and price loans accordingly.
[thoughtful] Paid by the formal companies the reform meant to help.

A state can spend the trust in its payment infrastructure exactly once, and Vietnam has just published the price. The part that travels: financial inclusion and fiscal legibility are the same infrastructure. Every state that built a QR rail on an inclusion story holds the same unexercised option. Vietnam exercised it first.
The banks say it’s just interest rates.

And they would know — the demand-deposit rate is regulated at around a tenth of a per cent against far higher term rates. We can’t settle it from published data, and the chain from reform to funding cost remains an inference. We say so.
And the one tell to watch?
If the state ever moves to compel merchants to accept digital payment. That’s the government conceding the rail is no longer a convenience it offers, but infrastructure it requires.
[pause] So the informal sector isn’t a transitional stage.
It’s a stable, chosen, rational form of economic life — and when you point a ledger at it, it has somewhere to go.
[warmly] What a book.
And our quote this morning is Carl Sagan. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
[chuckles] An unpublished treaty text. A statute never invoked.
That’s the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
